articles.title: India vs New Zealand | Henry Nicholls, Glenn Phillips stage stunning comback
articles.summary: Wellington: New Zealand have been a thorn in India’s flesh across formats over the last decade or so and Shubman Gill and Co felt that sharp sting once again on the first day of the opening Test. Just when Jasprit Bumrah’s mastery on a blustery and cold morning had the hosts shaken, Henry Nicholls and Glen Phillips scripted a sensational fightback to ensure the Black Caps took the honours on an absorbing day of cricket. Nicholls, who loves batting at the Basin Reserve, struck a majestic unbeaten 113 (221b, 14x4) to bring up his fifth Test century at the iconic venue and forged a superb unbroken 173-run partnership for the sixth wicket with the tenacious Phillips (94 n.o., 182b, 13x4) as New Zealand took stumps on Thursday at 243/5 in 82 overs. What the duo did, with Nicholls batting almost an entire day after arriving at the crease the third ball of the innings and Phillips defying the Indians for two sessions, was to turn Bumrah’s (3/52) individual brilliance into a footnote and ruthlessly expose India’s dubious decision to drop workhorse Mohammed Siraj. India vs New Zealand | Mohammed Siraj caught between red-ball priorities and ODI uncertainty Following a poor tour of New Zealand in 2020 where he picked up just 6 wickets in two Tests at a poor strike rate of 61.6, Bumrah meant business right from the get-go. With a chilly wind billowing across the venue and the pitch sporting a good amount of grass, Bumrah sent back skipper Tom Latham for a duck with a peach of a delivery. Latham shouldered arms to a ball that pitched on off stump and appeared headed away but to the southpaw’s dismay it just swung in marginally to rattle his stumps. Anshul Kamboj (1/57), the surprise pick over Siraj, impressed in his first spell by dismissing Devon Conway before Rachin Ravindra played a horrendous shot to gift his wicket to leave New Zealand in a spot at 51/3. Bumrah then had New Zealand under the mat with superb spells either side of lunch. Before the break he sent back the dangerous Daryl Mitchell with an intelligent bit of bowling and field placing. Noticing Mitchell was stepping down the track repeatedly, Bumrah placed a forward short leg and bowled into the batter’s body. Cramped for room, Mitchell ended up edging the ball to Yashasvi Jaiswal. India vs New Zealand | Windy Wellington poses a tough challenge for visitors After lunch, Bumrah dismissed Tom Blundell as India looked on course to blowing apart New Zealand — then 70/5 — on the opening day itself. But with the sun coming out and the pitch becoming a little easier to bat, India fluffed the lines inexplicably to let the day drift away with the guilty parties being Kamboj, Prasidh Krishna and Akash to some extent. Kamboj, just like his debut Test in Manchester last year, was all over the place after the first spell. He had no control over his lines or lengths and his pace dropped from mid 130 kmph to early 120 kmph as the day wore on. Prasidh too endured a horrendous day in the office, giving away a boundary ball every over. Kamboj and Prasidh inaccuracies ended up making life easy for Nicholls and Phillips and the New Zealand duo accepted the gifts gleefully. Both were aware that a bad ball was round the corner, so they defended the decent ones but made no mistake in punishing the bad deliveries. articles.title: Ariyil Shukkoor murder: 13 found guilty; CPI(M) leaders Jayarajan, Rajesh acquitted
articles.summary: Eighteen accused, including senior leaders of Communist Party of India (Marxist) P Jayarajan and TV Rajesh, were acquitted in the murder case of Ariyil Shukkoor, a member of the Muslim Students Federation (MSF). A special CBI court in Kochi on Thursday, November 19, found 13 persons guilty in the case. The quantum of the sentence will be pronounced at 3 PM. Shukkoor, 18, was murdered on February 20, 2012 by a vigilante mob, following an attack on the vehicle used by Jayarajan and Rajesh to visit Pattuvam in Kannur during a League-CPI(M) conflict. Jayarajan, then Kannur district secretary of CPI(M) and Rajesh, then an MLA, were accused of conspiracy in the murder. According to reports, Shukkoor was subjected to a ‘Kangaroo court’ trial for around two hours by the CPI(M) workers before he was stabbed to death. Special judge CBI-III (Ernakulam) P Sabarinathan found accused Sumesh KV, Anoop, Pavithran P, Manoharan PV, NP Ajith Kumar, P P Suresan, EP Radhakrishnan, Shijin Mohan @ Shijin, KV Sajith, VV Mohanan, Purushothaman MV @ Purushu, P K Ajith Kumar, and P P Suresan as guilty. Two accused passed away during trial. ‘Acquittal not on merit’: Special Prosecutor As per the case, Jayarajan and Rajesh, the 32nd and 33rd accused, were aware that Shukkoor was in the custody of CPI(M) workers and did nothing to prevent the murder. Both were charged with Section 118 of the Indian Penal Code (concealing a design to commit an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life). Special prosecutor K Padmanaban said that two crucial witnesses in the case refused to turn up for the trial. “The acquittals of 32nd and 33nd accused were not on merit. They were acquitted only because witnesses were not examined at the court. The 22nd and 23 witnesses refused to attend the trial. One witness is abroad. CBI served multiple notices for the second witness, but he remained absconding. The Kerala society must ask why this happened,” he said. Prosecution lawyers said that they are not satisfied, especially regarding the acquittal of second accused Ganesh. “As per the postmortem report, A1 (accused 1) stabbed on chest and A2 (accused 2) on stomach. Those two were fatal injuries. The weapon used by the accused, which was recovered following his confession, was produced in the court. There were blood stains on the weapon. An appeal will be filed against acquittal of the second accused,” lawyers said. Shyamjith, son of CPI(M) state general secretary MV Govindan, who was the 19th accused, too was acquitted. Speaking to the media after the verdict, Jayarajan alleged that the case was framed by League leadership to cause a mistrust among the minority community towards the CPI(M) leaders. Jayarajan said that a former Indian Police Service officer, who later joined the BJP, was behind adding section 118 against him and Rajesh. Jayarajan also alleged that a former judge of Kerala High Court took a biased stand. Rajesh asked why prosecution failed to bring the witnesses to court. “It is a politically fabricated case,” he said. CPI(M) Kannur district secretary K K Ragesh said the allegation of a CPI(M) kangaroo court was a media creation. State industries minister and Indian Union Muslim league general secretary PK Kunhalikutty said that there was no doubt that Shukkoor murder was a planned one. “Everyone knows that the witness failed to appear before the court due to fear. An appeal should be filed to prove the conspiracy angle,” he said.

articles.title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
articles.summary: By Brian Melley Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist. “Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people. “AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children." The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.” Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning. Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years. “AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method. “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.” Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.

articles.title: Rohingya crisis remains unresolved as ICJ rules on Myanmar
articles.summary: The United Nations' highest court will hand down a long-awaited judgment on Thursday in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Muslim Rohingya population. The decision comes nearly a decade after a 2017 military crackdown drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh, and as conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable. Explained | How is genocide proven in court? Why did the Rohingya flee Myanmar? More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the United Nations. The largest displacement began in August 2017, when Myanmar's armed forces launched an offensive following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army insurgent group on about 30 police posts and an army base. The military crackdown forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee into Bangladesh. Refugees described mass killings, gang rapes, torture and the burning of hundreds of villages, according to Human Rights Watch. Myanmar's government denied the allegations, saying its forces were targeting militants. What is the ICJ case against Myanmar? In 2019, Gambia filed a case at the ICJ, also known as the World Court, backed by the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, alleging that Myanmar's 2017 military offensive in Rakhine State amounted to genocide. The ICJ judgments are final and binding, but the court has limited means of enforcement and cannot convict individuals or issue arrest warrants. In 2019 preliminary hearings in the ICJ case, Myanmar's then leader, Aung San Suu Kyi, rejected Gambia's accusations of genocide as "incomplete and misleading". The ICJ in January 2020 ordered Myanmar to take urgent measures to protect Rohingya people remaining in the country, including preventing possible genocidal acts and preserving evidence. What is the situation in Rakhine? Myanmar's military, led by Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021. The overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million. As conflict spread, renewed fighting between Myanmar's military junta and the Arakan Army rebel group broke out in Rakhine State in November 2023, forcing more Rohingya civilians to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh. The minority group has also faced attacks by the Arakan Army, which set alight swathes of the Rohingya settlement of Buthidaung in May 2024, Reuters has reported. Jammu land drive puts Myanmar’s Rohingya refugees in fresh uncertainty Why can't the Rohingya return? As conflict rages on in Rakhine, conditions for the safe return of Rohingya refugees do not currently exist, according to aid groups. Myanmar said in August that it had verified 308,797 people living in displacement camps in Bangladesh as former residents of Rakhine State, but repatriation would begin only when security conditions in Rakhine improve. Some Rohingya refugees say they are not willing to go back without full rights, dignity, and citizenship. Myanmar's government has long seen the Rohingya as illegal migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh and denied them citizenship, even though Rohingya families have lived there for generations. Earlier repatriation plans in 2018 and 2019 resulted in no returns.

articles.title: Official records need not separately identify children as adopted, Kerala HC says
articles.summary: The Kerala High Court has directed the state government to remove the option of describing a person as an ‘adopted son’ or ‘adopted daughter’ in official documents, ruling that adopted children must be recognised simply as the son or daughter of their adoptive parents. Justice P V Kunhikrishnan issued the direction while allowing a petition filed by a woman, who challenged a legal heirship certificate that described her as the ‘adopted daughter’ of her deceased father instead of simply ‘daughter’. The judgement was delivered on November 10, 2026. The court directed the government to modify the guidelines and the e-District portal to remove the option that allows revenue authorities to separately identify an heir as an adopted child. The changes must be made within one month of receiving a certified copy of the judgement. “An adopted child shall be deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the date of the adoption,” the court observed, referring to Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. The judge said that once a child is adopted, the law recognises the child as the son or daughter of the adoptive parents, and there is no necessity to distinguish them from biological children in official records. “Therefore, society will accept a child adopted by a person as the child of the adoptive parents. When society treats the child as the son or daughter of the adoptive parents, there is no need to describe the child as an ‘adopted girl’ or ‘adopted boy’ in official documents,” the judgement said. The court further clarified, “There is no insult in describing a child as an adopted son or adopted daughter, which is statutorily recognised, but the same should be avoided while recording in official documents,” Justice Kunhikrishnan observed. The petitioner was adopted on June 30, 1990, when she was less than a month old, by a couple who had remained childless after more than 16 years of marriage. The adoption was carried out through a court order. According to the judgement, she was accepted and treated as the daughter of her adoptive parents in all respects from the date of adoption. Her relationship with them was also reflected as a daughter in official documents, including her Aadhaar, passport, ration card, electoral identity card, driving licence, PAN card and SSLC certificate. After her adoptive mother died on January 3, 2023, the tahsildar issued a legal heirship certificate on March 16, 2023, recognising the petitioner as her sole legal heir and describing her as ‘daughter’. Her adoptive father died on October 15, 2024. The village officer subsequently issued a family membership certificate describing her as his daughter. However, when the Tahsildar issued a legal heirship certificate for her father on June 28, 2025, the petitioner was described as his ‘adopted daughter’. She approached the High Court seeking to set aside the certificate to the extent that it described her as an adopted daughter and to direct the authorities to issue a fresh certificate identifying her simply as his daughter. The petitioner contended that the additional description was unnecessary and adversely affected her legal status and dignity. She also pointed out that the authorities had not made any such distinction in the certificates issued earlier in respect of her mother and father. State says it was following guidelines The state government, in its counter-affidavit, submitted that an enquiry had established that the petitioner was an adopted child. It said the government had issued guidelines for issuing legal heirship certificates and that the e-District portal provided a specific option to record whether a legal heir was an adopted son or daughter. The government argued that the option had been provided to ensure uniformity and accuracy in certificates issued by revenue authorities and that the Tahsildar was merely following the existing guidelines. However, the court rejected the argument. Referring to section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, the judge reiterated that an adopted child is deemed to be the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes from the date of adoption, with the ties to the birth family severed and replaced by those created in the adoptive family, subject to the statutory exceptions. The court said the government should immediately remove the option from the e-District portal. “In the official records, no child shall be described as an ‘adopted son or daughter.’ Such children should be shown as ‘son’ or ‘daughter’. No prefix is necessary,” the judgment said. New certificates Allowing the writ petition, the High Court set aside the legal heirship certificate issued to the petitioner's father and directed the Thrissur tahsildar to issue a fresh certificate describing her relationship with her deceased father as ‘daughter’ instead of ‘adopted daughter’. The certificate must be issued forthwith and, in any case, within two weeks of receiving a certified copy of the judgment. The court also directed the government to amend the e-District portal guidelines within one month, deleting the option that requires an adopted child to be separately identified in legal heirship certificates.

articles.title: Van Gogh’s ‘Chataigniers en Fleurs’ sells at auction for record $190.4 million
articles.summary: Vincent van Gogh's 1890 painting "Chataigniers en Fleurs," a radiant depiction of village life unseen in public for more than 50 years, was sold to a bidder on Wednesday for $190.4 million, an auction record for the famed Post-Impressionist. Sotheby's of New York, which held the auction, said the sum also marked the second-highest price paid for any work of art sold by its auction house, surpassed only by Gustav Klimt's "Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer," which sold in November 2025 for $236.4 million. Announcing the sale in a press statement, the auction house made no mention of the buyer. But the New York Times reported the prevailing bidder was William Acquavella, a veteran art dealer and the head of Acquavella Galleries. Van Gogh painted the canvas, dominated by a lush row of flowering chestnut trees lining a village road, days after he arrived in the French hamlet of Auvers-sur-Oise, northwest of Paris, where he spent the final two months of his life. Tracing the origin of 'The Starry Night' The composition features a solitary male figure in a hat, thought to possibly represent the artist himself, walking past a trio of colorfully dressed women carrying parasols in the shade of the trees. The vibrantly worked brush strokes are said to connect the painting with other celebrated works of this period in van Gogh's career, including "The Starry Night" and "The Church at Auvers-sur-Oise." Sotheby's characterized the painting as one of the most important works from that era of van Gogh's career remaining in private hands, and "among the most exceptional Post-Impressionist paintings ever to come to the market." The van Gogh painting was part of a larger group of 12 masterpieces auctioned on Wednesday from the renowned Blaquier-Arrieta Collection of Impressionist and Modern paintings. "Chataigniers en Fleurs" had remained out of public view for more than a half century, since the Argentina-based Blaquier family acquired it 1975, according to Sotheby's. The masterpiece was offered for sale under an agreement reached between the Blaquier family and heirs of the painting's former owner, Hungarian-born German Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer, to settle the family's claim that he had sold the painting in the 1930s under duress of Nazi persecution. Seven powerful anti-war paintings that capture the true tragedy of conflict Sotheby's, which said it helped broker the deal, did not disclose terms of the agreement. All 12 works auctioned from the collection sold for a total of $412 million, against Sotheby’s estimated value of roughly $450 million. One of those paintings, Paul Cezanne's "Harlequin," went for $111 million, with fees. The $190.4 million paid on Wednesday for “Chataigniers en Fleurs” exceeded the previous van Gogh auction record of $117.2 million, fetched in 2022 at Christie’s for the landscape "Verger avec Cypres," from the collection of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, Sotheby's said.

articles.title: Tech outages are piling up, and AI is raising the stakes. Could this be the new normal?
articles.summary: By Wyatte Grantham-philips, Kelvin Chan And Kaitlyn Huamani Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays . And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions . In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal . Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft , JP Morgan Chase and Apple , and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency . The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. “To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.” What's gone offline recently Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved. And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app. Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.” The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there's no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack. Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents," although it didn't immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email. AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps. For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP , a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays. President Donald Trump's director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA's outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month's PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said. Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it. At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions. “As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week. He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.” While recent outages haven't been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly. “AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering. In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them. Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services. Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era. “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges. Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

articles.title: Nuclear arms and ending wars in Iran and Ukraine will top the agenda at Trump-Xi-Putin meeting
articles.summary: By Josh Boak, Michelle L. Price And E. Eduardo Castillo President Donald Trump meets on Thursday with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, a moment that could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op. Trump, who will test his reputation as an expert dealmaker in the trilateral meeting, has promoted his time with Xi and Putin — two of America's leading rivals — as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs. Trump had a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi — his third substantial meeting with him this year — right before the trilateral. The U.S. president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America. “I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” Trump said. Xi said that relations between the United States and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. “The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said. The meeting between Trump and Xi lasted roughly an hour, after which the two leaders and their delegations had lunch. Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin to his schedule, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine . “Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said after joining Putin for the one-on-one meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit , calling Putin “my friend." “We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting together lasted roughly 40 minutes. Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin , even as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions , while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war. Along for the trip — but so far keeping a low profile — is Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX has intermittently throttled the military-grade Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for launching its drones and intercepting hits from Russia. One meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough in nuclear talks Trump has said he wants to talk to the leaders about their nuclear stockpiles. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China . But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said Trump's showmanship could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals. “We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at APEC," Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.” Trump told Fox News in his interview that “it’s a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles. Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger The U.S. president's ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or countries like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks. The U.S. president has openly pursued a Nobel Peace Prize even as he took military action against Venezuela and Iran. Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi appealed to his ego Wednesday by greeting Air Force One on the airport tarmac, as the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug. But Trump does not appear to always have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. For all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutually effusive. On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions. By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi plan to meet a total of four times this year, with their final time together coming in December at the G20 summit being held at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida. Ukraine and its European allies are suspicious of the trilateral meeting that could potentially cut them out of the process. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another “Anchorage moment,” a reference to last year's Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners. Conflicts on AI and trade also hang over the meetings While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world's two largest economies. China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the U.S. has almost equally large trade deficits. And the race between the U.S. and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks. Trump ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped to give China access to the company's advanced computer chips used to develop AI models. Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent. Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China's ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to insult China and aggravate relations. Before APEC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. The U.S. officials said afterward that China had not fully honored its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more U.S. agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics. The trade truce between the U.S. and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan. 10 next year. Trump officials have dangled the possibility of opening up highly sanctioned trade with Russia as an incentive for ending hostilities in Ukraine, and Trump has frequently demonstrated that he sees trade as a foreign policy tool. Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the U.S. war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth.

articles.title: Health ministry proposes amendment to drug rules to bring antimicrobials under regulatory oversight
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed bringing antimicrobials under the Central regulatory framework applicable to new drugs to strengthen oversight of their quality, safety and efficacy and address antimicrobial resistance (AMR). It has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, through a draft gazette notification dated November 6, seeking to include antimicrobials in the definition of new drug under Rule 2(1)(w)(v). AMR is a major global public health concern and a priority requiring coordinated action, the ministry said. Centre proposes immediate suspension of manufacturing licenses when drugs fail quality tests The G20 New Delhi Leaders' Declaration also underscored the need to address antimicrobial resistance through a ‘One Health’ approach. “The proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability/bioequivalence and stability studies,” the ministry said. “The absence of such assessments may affect the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products. Substandard or ineffective antimicrobials can contribute to the development and spread of antimicrobial resistance, posing risks to patient safety,” it added. The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the 2019 rules. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority (SLA). This is expected to strengthen the Central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products, the ministry said. The draft notification invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public before the proposed amendment is considered for finalisation by the Centre. Antimicrobials are agents that kill microorganisms or stop their growth. They include medicines used to treat or prevent infections, as well as substances applied to skin or surfaces to reduce microbes.

Displays are representing the Toda, Munda, Soliga, Alu Kurumba, Sora, Gondi and Ulladan communities, along with CIIL's institutional display. articles.title: Supreme Court to commence final hearing of pleas on marital rape in December
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Thursday said it would list a batch of petitions pertaining to the contentious issue of marital rape for final hearing in December. The apex court is seized of petitions raising the vexed legal question of whether a husband should enjoy immunity from prosecution for the offence of rape if he forces his wife, who is not a minor, to have sex. Under the exception clause of Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code, now repealed and replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his wife, the wife not being minor, is not rape. Will fix date in marital rape petitions after Centre's stand on issue: Supreme Court Marital rape debate reaches Supreme Court: Can husbands be prosecuted under existing law? Even under the new law, exception 2 to section 63 (rape) says that "sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape". The petitions were listed for hearing during the day before a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. Senior advocate Indira Jaising, who is appearing in the matter, told the apex court that the bench is scheduled to hear a part-heard matter at 2 pm during the day. She urged the bench that the marital rape matter be listed for hearing in December as today it may not come up since the bench is seized of a part-heard matter. "We will either have it on December 2-3 or on December 9-10. Today, it is not possible. We are trying to finish the part-heard matter today," the CJI said. One of the lawyers appearing in the marital rape case requested the bench to list the matter on December 9 and 10. "We will fix it on December 9 or December 10," the bench said, adding, "We will try to hear it before the winter break". The winter break in the apex court would commence from December 21. On September 9, the Centre had told the bench that the counter affidavit filed earlier by it in the lead case may be treated as its reply in other petitions as well. The bench had then observed that it would examine aspects such as whether prosecution can be sustained if the marital rape exception survives, and whether the exception itself was constitutionally valid. The top court had on January 16, 2023 sought the Centre's response on a clutch of petitions assailing the IPC provision which provides protection to a husband against prosecution for forcible sexual intercourse if the wife is an adult. Later, it also issued notice to the Centre on a similar plea challenging the BNS provision on the issue. The newly enacted laws — the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam — came into effect from July 1, 2024, replacing the IPC, the CrPC and the Evidence Act. One of pleas in the apex court arises from the Delhi High Court's split verdict of May 11, 2022 on the issue. The appeal has been filed by a woman, who was one of the petitioners before the high court. While delivering a split judgement, high court judges Justice Rajiv Shakdher and Justice C Hari Shankar had concurred on granting the petitioners a certificate of leave to appeal in the Supreme Court as the matter involved substantial questions of law that required a decision by the top court. While Justice Shakdher, who headed the division bench, favoured striking down the marital rape exception for being "unconstitutional" and said it would be "tragic if a married woman's call for justice is not heard even after 162 years" since the enactment of the IPC, Justice Shankar said the exception under the rape law is not "unconstitutional and was based on an intelligible differentia". In a separate matter, the Karnataka High Court has earlier said exempting a husband from the allegations of rape and unnatural sex with his wife runs against Article 14 (equality before law) of the Constitution.

The coastal and southern regions of the state have been experiencing light to moderate rain since Wednesday night, and the intensity will increase gradually, they said. As a precautionary measure, the railway authorities have cancelled two trains between Visakhapatnam and Koraput on Thursday and Friday. Odisha govt evacuates nearly 50,000 people as cyclone 'Akvan' shifts course towards state Cyclone Akvan intensifies into severe cyclonic storm, landfall between Machilipatnam and Puri on Nov 20 The uncertainty over the landfall location was cleared by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) in its morning bulletin, saying that the system is likely to cross north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri, close to east of Gopalpur, by Friday noon with the maximum sustained wind speed of 90-100 kmph, gusting to 110 kmph. "Keeping in view of the weather forecast, the state government has sped up evacuation exercises and has so far shifted more than 80,000 people to safety against its target of 2 lakh," a Revenue and Disaster Management Department official said. The state government has closed educational institutes in districts marked under 'red' (take action), 'orange' (be prepared) and 'yellow' (be aware) warnings, another official said, adding that 74 rescue teams have been deployed in Malkangiri, Koraput, Rayagada, Kalahandi, Gajapati, Ganjam, Kandhamal, Boudh, Puri, Nayagarh and Khurda districts. As Ganjam is likely to be the worst hit by the impending cyclone, the district administration has shifted 36,398 people to shelters by 6 am on Thursday, and evacuation is underway, an official said. Altogether, 308 shelters are operational, with free kitchens serving the evacuated people, he said, adding that 1,098 pregnant women have been shifted safely. Four teams of Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF), three of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), 24 of Fire and Emergency Services and 10 of Odisha Forest Development Corporation (OFDC) have been deployed across all blocks of Ganjam, the district official said. The IMD, in its morning bulletin, said that the severe cyclonic storm 'Akvan' over the west-central Bay of Bengal moved northwards at a speed of 12 kmph during the past six hours till 5.30 am, and lay centred at about 440 km east-southeast of Narsapur (Andhra Pradesh), 530 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha) and 590 km south of Puri (Odisha). The Met office issued a red warning for Kendrapara, Jagatsinghpur, Puri, Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal districts for Thursday, forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall. A storm surge of 0.5 to 1 metre above the astronomical tide is likely to inundate low-lying areas of Ganjam and Puri districts, the weather office said. Strong winds are expected along the south and north Odisha coasts as the cyclone approaches. The IMD said squally winds of 40-50 kmph, gusting up to 60 kmph in south Odisha, are currently prevailing across the coast.

articles.title: Kashmir’s counter-terror crackdown: Where does security end and due process begin?
articles.summary: Srinagar: The demolition of houses belonging to alleged militants, attachment of properties suspected to be linked to terrorism and dismissal of government employees accused of militant connections have become important components of Jammu and Kashmir’s counter-terror strategy. But a series of judicial interventions has brought into focus a larger question: where does the state’s security imperative end and an individual’s right to due process begin? The measures, intended to dismantle the financial, logistical and institutional networks supporting militancy, increasingly extend counter-terror action beyond armed militants to their alleged facilitators and support structures. 'Collective punishment only breeds alienation': Mehbooba Mufti on search operation by security forces In July, following the killing of a police head constable in Anantnag, authorities demolished the houses of two alleged militants in south Kashmir. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah questioned the action, referring to Supreme Court guidelines against summary demolition of properties. PDP president Mehbooba Mufti also criticised the demolitions, describing them as collective punishment. The administration’s actions extend to government employees accused of links with militant organisations. Article 311(2)(c) of the Constitution empowers the Lieutenant Governor, exercising the Governor’s constitutional powers in J&K, to dismiss a government employee without a departmental inquiry if satisfied that holding one would not be expedient in the interest of state security. The provision is an exception to the normal safeguards available to government employees facing disciplinary action. High Court quashes Jammu and Kashmir Bank officer’s dismissal over alleged anti-India campaign J&K govt begins fresh identification of ‘terror-linked’ employees The legal debate has gained prominence following the case of Saadut Hussain Pampori, a former Deputy General Manager of J&K Bank, who was dismissed in July 2024 over alleged involvement in anti-national activities. In August 2026, the J&K High Court quashed his termination, observing that dismissal without an inquiry was a drastic measure that should be used only in appropriate cases. Justice Sanjay Dhar held that the bank had failed to establish the investigation required under Clause 12.29 of its Officers Service Manual. The court allowed the bank to initiate fresh proceedings after following the prescribed procedure or conduct a regular departmental inquiry. The ruling, however, was challenged by the bank. A Division Bench stayed the operation of the single-judge order on September 14, 2026. Property attachment under Section 25 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) follows a separate legal procedure. It allows authorities to seize or attach property believed to represent proceeds of terrorism, subject to prescribed approvals and review. In G M Bhat vs State of J&K (2023), Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal examined the safeguards under Section 25. The High Court held that statutory timelines for reviewing attachment orders must be followed and that an appellate authority cannot extend the prescribed period by remanding a matter. It observed that the authority “ought to have exercised the power … by revoking such order of the designated authority and releasing the property”. The Supreme Court’s November 2024 guidelines on demolitions have also prescribed safeguards, including prior notice, an opportunity to respond and compliance with due process. The apex court cautioned against demolishing a family home merely because one occupant is accused or convicted of an offence.

articles.title: No objection if ex-SC judge acts as mediator in Krishna-Godavari basin gas migration dispute: Centre to Supreme Court
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Centre on Thursday told the Supreme Court that it has no objection to former top court judge Ranjana Prakash Desai acting as the sole mediator in the Krishna-Godavari basin gas migration dispute involving Reliance Industries and others. Attorney General R Venkataramani, appearing for the Centre, told a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that Justice Desai had some apprehension that the government had an objection to her mediating the dispute. “We had conveyed to her Ladyship that the government has no reservation,” the top-most law officer said. The CJI said that Justice Desai was appointed the mediator with the concurrence of both sides. Senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for a private party, said that besides Justice Desai, there have to be two domain experts in the mediation panel. The government has proposed the name of a former petroleum secretary as a domain expert, Sibal said, adding that though he has no objection to the former official, he should not be there if he has acted in his official capacity in this case. SC appoints former judge Ranjana Desai as sole mediator in KG basin gas dispute “The attorney general has assured us,” Sibal said, adding that they wanted an amicable resolution of this aspect. On October 30, the bench had appointed former Supreme Court judge Justice Desai as the sole mediator in the matter. “The parties themselves have not been able to find a viable solution. We suggest, on their behalf, that former judge of this court, Ranjana Prakash Desai, be requested to act as mediator. “We also request the learned mediator to have the assistance of two domain experts, as may be suggested by the parties, for the aforesaid purpose,” the bench had said. The attorney general had assured full cooperation to the mediator. “The parties may contact Hon'ble Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai during the course of the day or by tomorrow and fix the date and time as per his convenience,” the bench had said. On May 20, the apex court had declined a submission by Reliance Industries to put the hearing in the Krishna-Godavari basin gas migration dispute on hold for the time being as the company and two other foreign firms sought mediation or conciliation with the Centre for an amicable resolution. The top court was hearing the appeals of Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL), BP Exploration (Alpha) Ltd and Niko (NECO) Ltd against a Delhi High Court verdict that set aside an arbitral award in their favour in the gas migration dispute with the Centre. The firms assailed the February 14, 2025, order of the high court setting aside an order of the single-judge bench that had upheld the arbitral award in favour of RIL and its two partners for allegedly siphoning gas from deposits they had no right to exploit. In July 2018, an international arbitration tribunal had rejected the Indian government's claim of USD 1.55 billion against RIL and its partners for allegedly siphoning gas from deposits they had no right to exploit. The three-member arbitral panel, by a majority of 2-1, also awarded USD 8.3 million compensation to the three partners, Reliance had said in a regulatory filing. Earlier, a division bench of the high court had allowed the appeal of the Centre challenging a May 9, 2023, judgment of a single judge that was passed in favour of the Mukesh Ambani-promoted RIL. Upholding the arbitral award, the single judge had said the court was not persuaded to hold that the conclusions drawn by the arbitral tribunal were such that no reasonable person would reach. The oil ministry on November 4, 2016, slapped a demand of USD 1.47 billion on the Reliance-BP-Niko combine for producing in seven years ending March 31, 2016, about 338.332 million British thermal units of gas that had seeped or migrated from ONGC's blocks into their adjoining KG-D6 in the Bay of Bengal. After deducting USD 71.71 million royalty paid on the gas produced and adding interest at the rate of LIBOR plus 2 per cent, totalling USD 149.86 million, a total demand of USD 1.55 billion was made on Reliance, BP and Niko. Reliance had disputed the government's demand as being based on a “misreading and misinterpretation of key elements of the PSC”, and said that such a demand was without precedent in the oil and gas industry. On November 11, 2016, it sent an arbitration notice. Reliance is the operator of the KG-D6 block with a 60 per cent interest, while BP holds 30 per cent. The remaining 10 per cent is with Niko Resources. The government's compensation claim flowed from a report of the Justice A P Shah (retd) Committee. In its August 28, 2016, report, the Shah panel concluded that there had been “unjust enrichment” to the contractor of the block KG-DWN-98/3 (KG-D6) due to the production of migrated gas from ONGC's blocks KG-DWN-98/2 and Godavari PML. Originally, ONGC had sued Reliance for producing gas that had migrated from its blocks KG-DWN-98/2 (KG-D5) and Godavari PML in the KG basin to the adjoining KG-D6 block of Reliance. Under the direction of the Delhi High Court, the government had appointed a one-man committee under retired Justice Shah to go into the issue. Shah, however, said the compensation should go to the government as it is the owner of all unproduced natural resources.
